analysis.one_liner: Sets federal standards for managed care plans — on coverage denials, emergency care, and childbirth stays — enforced by a tax on insurers that fail.
analysis.headline: With no cosponsors and no committee action, the bill died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required managed care health plans to meet a list of consumer protections: doctors' coverage denials would have to be reviewed by qualified medical professionals and reviewers could not be paid based on how many claims they deny; emergency care would be covered without prior approval; mothers and newborns would get at least 48 hours in the hospital after a normal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean; and patients could not be kept from participating in approved clinical trials. Plans that failed to meet the standards would owe a tax equal to 25 percent of their premiums. It also tightened rules for Medicare supplement (Medigap) insurance — requiring community rating, raising the share of premiums that must go back to benefits from 75 to 85 percent, and barring denial of coverage for people with pre-existing conditions in many cases — and added orientation and immunization requirements for Medicare and Medicaid managed care.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries. Patients would get fairer review of denied claims, guaranteed access to emergency rooms and specialists, disclosure of how plans pay doctors, and minimum hospital stays after childbirth. People with chronic illnesses would get access to centers of excellence, and Medicare beneficiaries would get stronger Medigap protections, including guaranteed issue for people whose coverage ended through no fault of their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Managed care enrollees and Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Plans could not deny or pay less for services based on a utilization review program unless it was certified by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and reviewers could not be paid based on the number of denials [S2].
Plans had to cover emergency services without prior authorization and regardless of whether the provider was in the plan's network [S2].

Plans offering childbirth coverage had to provide at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, or cover timely post-delivery follow-up care at home [S3].

Plans had to assure timely access to a sufficient number and variety of providers, give enrollees access to designated centers of excellence for chronic conditions, and cover routine care for enrollees in approved clinical studies [S2].
Plans could not restrict or retaliate against doctors for discussing treatment options, the basis for coverage decisions, or the plan's financial incentives with patients [S3].

Plans had to provide grievance procedures and independent appeal panels, respond to urgent coverage requests within 24 hours, and give enrollees standardized information on coverage, quality, and physician incentive arrangements [S2] [S3].
A plan or insurer that failed the requirements would owe an excise tax of 25 percent of the premiums received for the plan year [S3].

Medigap issuers would have had to return at least 85 percent of premiums as benefits (up from 75 percent), use community rating, guarantee issue to people losing prior coverage, and hold an annual open enrollment period without pre-existing-condition exclusions [S2].

Medicare and Medicaid managed care organizations would not receive payments for an enrollee until they provided required orientation and medical profiling, and Medicaid plans had to ensure childhood immunizations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and health insurance companies, which would face the 25-percent-of-premiums excise tax for failures, restrictions on how they pay utilization reviewers and agents, guaranteed-network and emergency-coverage requirements, and expanded disclosure. Medigap issuers would bear the higher 85 percent loss ratio and guaranteed-issue requirements. To the extent these costs are passed on, employers and enrollees could face somewhat higher premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Managed care plans and health insurers

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism is an excise tax of 25 percent of a plan's entire annual premiums for any uncorrected failure, a steep penalty that insurers and employers would argue raises the cost of coverage [S3].

The bill requires Health and Human Services to certify utilization review programs and set detailed standards, adding federal administrative oversight of how private plans make medical coverage decisions [S2].
Mandated benefits such as minimum hospital stays after childbirth and guaranteed-access rules add costs that insurers would say show up in premiums for all enrollees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections address real, documented problems of 1990s managed care: claim denials driven by reviewer incentives, barriers to emergency care and specialists, and 'drive-through' childbirth stays. The cost is heavier regulation and the threat of a 25-percent-of-premiums tax on plans, which could push up premiums. The design — enforcing patient protections through the tax code rather than through a new regulatory agency — is unusual and would have made penalties severe, though it included reasonable-cause waivers and 30-day correction windows. Many of these ideas were later adopted in narrower form by federal and state law, which suggests the core protections were workable even if this particular bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late September 1996 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce committees and then to a Commerce subcommittee; neither committee ever acted, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark of California introduced the Managed Care Consumer Protection Act of 1996 on September 26, 1996 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Commerce, each for the portions within its jurisdiction [S5].
On October 22, 1996, the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the Senate, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans and insurers came out ahead: they avoided the excise tax, the utilization-review and disclosure rules, and the Medigap changes, while the patients who would have gained the protections received none.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would tax plans 25 percent of premiums for failing consumer-protection standards, ban paying coverage reviewers by the number of denials, and require guaranteed emergency coverage, disclosure of physician incentive arrangements, and grievance procedures. Those rules would cost the industry money that patients would otherwise bear through denied care.

The bill would raise the minimum share of premiums returned as benefits from 75 to 85 percent, require community rating, guarantee issue to people losing prior coverage, and mandate annual open enrollment without pre-existing-condition exclusions — shrinking underwriting profits and flexibility [S2].

Commissions for enrolling people in managed care plans could no longer be the predominant part of an agent's pay, and commissions would have to be recouped if a new enrollee left within 90 days — limiting enrollment-driven commission income [S3].
